title: Bridging ML and algorithms: comparison of hyperbolic embeddings
claim: Hyperbolic space can be tiled by regular polygons in different ways, giving distinct structures that fill the disk toward the boundary.
layout: 3 panels side by side, left-to-right, Poincaré disks with shrinking cells toward edge
description: Three Poincaré disks are shown side by side, each filled with a different tessellation of the hyperbolic plane in black line art on white. The left disk shows a sparse tiling of large pentagon-like cells whose curved edges thicken near the center and break into ever smaller cells toward the boundary circle. The middle disk shows a heptagonal tiling: a central heptagon surrounded by rings of heptagons that shrink rapidly toward the thin blue-black rim. The right disk shows the bitruncated order-3 heptagonal tiling, in which gray-shaded large heptagons alternate with smaller white polygons. Shading is the only color device. The eye goes first to the central cell in each disk and then outward to the dense fine mesh at the edges. The figure has no labels, arrows or text.
caption: Tessellations of the hyperbolic plane. Bitruncated order-3 heptagonal tiling on the right.
abstract: Hyperbolic embeddings are well-studied in the machine learning, network theory, and algorithm communities. However, as the research proceeds independently in those communities, comparisons and even awareness seem to be currently lacking. We compare the performance (computation time) and the quality of embeddings obtained by popular approaches as of 2025, both on real-life hierarchies and networks, and simulated networks. According to our results, the algorithm by Bläsius et al (ESA 2016) is about 100 times faster than the Poincar\'e embeddings (NIPS 2017) and Lorentz embeddings (ICML 2018) by Nickel and Kiela, while achieving results of similar (or, in some cases, even better) quality.
